doc.title: Jane Ira Bloom interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 3, 1998

title: Tune titles, inspiration and putting a stamp on standards
summary: Her titles reflect 1990s interests and act as springboards; she reshapes standards like those on The Nearness.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: As long as we’re talking about that I’ve noticed that the titles of your own tunes seem to have some significance rather than just, you know, Jane’s Blues, or things like that. And in fact when we heard you in New York you seem to have a wide range of things that may affect your compositions. For instance there was a football theme.
NFL. How do you get your inspiration?

Well it’s a wide, pretty wide span of interests I have. I think because I think that it’s an improviser’s job to reflect and react to their own time, that those titles reflects the scope of things that interest me today, you know, in the 1990s. And I let them affect what I think about as a jazz player. And the titles, I think of them more like I suppose the way a poet would think about them. They’re kind of like springboards for your imagination you know. I never like to explain them, I like to let the music speak for itself. But they speak of something that’s been going on in my head about why I wrote these pieces. You have to sort of take it from there.

Okay. Well there’s an almost programmatic, at least one of the tunes I heard, you had the drummer blowing a whistle and I really liked it. And it was different than obviously the typical situation which we probably will have tonight with you, where you’re kind of thrown in with musicians you haven’t played with before and it’s pretty much okay what standards do we know — which is great to hear from the pros — but to hear a rehearsed group that’s actually playing original work, I thought it was very refreshing.

Sure. Even when you do play the standards it’s always been my point of view to just kind of say something important about why you’re playing them. You know you sort of put a different spin on them because of why you’re playing them, in 1998, and it’s not 1930 or 1940 anymore. So it makes sense to me to kind of put your stamp on whatever you do.
As you did on your last album.
“The Nearness.” Some of that work seems to back up what you’re saying.

Sure. No I love the music of this tradition you know. All the standards that I perform like “‘Round Midnight,” or “The Nearness of You,” or what else did I play on that one, “Lonely House,” these are beautiful melodies, jazz ballads, and I just thought it was kind of interesting to shape them in a sort of different way.
